executive_summary: The $2.0M is prepaid royalty, not new revenue; net of OEM costs, exclusivity earns $3.2M over three years at plan, $1.0M at 65% – Booking the advance on top of royalties overstates the deal by 23% – At 2027 plan volume, $40 of each $300 royalty is left after OEM costs (p. 4–6)

Exclusivity bars new direct licensing; at 65% of volumes it loses money in 2028 once over 36% of direct profit is lost – $1.48M of 2028 direct gross profit is at stake, with no data on how much goes – The growth case rests on five correlational cases and an unbooked forecast (p. 8, 9)

Exclusivity at signing breaks the board's own conditions, and the work is fundable without the advance – Lab downtime ran at 2.4 times the OEM's limit, and the draft lacks six protections – Without the advance, a year of OEM costs leaves $0.55M above the buffer (p. 11–13)

Sign the nonexclusive pilot; grant limited exclusivity only after certification and audited volume – Pilot terms match exclusivity in 2028 even with a third fewer robots – Shipments, direct loss, support cost or audit rights could change it (p. 15–18)

slides.title: What the deal is worth
The $2.0M signing payment is prepaid royalty, not new revenue: counting it on top would overstate the deal by 23%

claims.claim: The advance moves cash forward; it adds nothing to the total
evidence: Royalties earned, $M: 2027 1.5; 2028 3; 2029 4.2
Royalties and cash both total $8.7M over 2027–29 at plan volumes
The $2.0M is an advance minimum guarantee credited against the first $2.0M of earned royalties; royalties count only when robots ship, and cash arrives after a reporting lag

claims.claim: 23% overstatement of three-year value if the advance is booked on top of royalties
2027: the advance absorbs all of the year's royalties
2028: cash trails royalties while the unused credit is netted
At 65% of plan: 2027 royalties use under half the advance, and the OEM can demand an offset

slides.title: At 2027 plan volumes, support and the dedicated OEM team absorb most of each royalty, leaving $40 of the $300

claims.claim: The dashboard's margin is not the deal's margin
evidence: Per robot: Royalty $300; Variable support $80; Dedicated OEM team $180; Left per robot $40
13.3% of each royalty is left at 2027 plan volume, against the 100% margin the CFO dashboard reports

claims.claim: Support: the dashboard leaves out the $80 support cost on every robot shipped
Dedicated team: $0.9M a year of engineering, quality and support, a fixed cost spread over few robots in 2027
evidence: Dedicated team cost per robot = $0.9M a year ÷ 5,000 robots in the 2027 partner forecast

claims.claim: Volume: the team is covered only above about 4,091 robots a year, which the 65% stress case misses
evidence: 4,091 robots a year

claims.claim: the dashboard's 100% margin also leaves out the direct sales exclusivity would give up

slides.title: Net of all OEM costs, three years of exclusivity contribute $3.2M at plan but only $1.0M at 65% of volumes

claims.claim: At plan, fixed and variable costs take nearly two-thirds of royalties
evidence: Plan, $M: Royalties 8.7; Support 2.32; OEM team 2.7; Assessment 0.45; Net 3.23

claims.claim: At 65% of plan, the same fixed costs leave about a sixth of royalties
evidence: 65% of plan, $M: Royalties 5.65; Support 1.508; OEM team 2.7; Assessment 0.45; Net 0.992

claims.claim: Fixed costs do not shrink with volume, so a 35% shortfall in shipments wipes out more than two-thirds of the deal's value
evidence: the $0.9M team is counted for all three years and the $0.45M safety assessment once, in 2027
Support at $80 a robot on 29,000 planned robots (18,850 at 65%)
Before any direct sales lost to exclusivity

slides.title: What exclusivity gives up
Exclusivity's 2028 value hinges on direct sales nobody has measured: at 65% of volumes it turns negative above 36% lost

claims.claim: The answer turns on a number the pipeline cannot yet show
evidence: Plan volumes, $M by share of 2028 direct gross profit lost: 0% (CEO view) 1.3; 30% (Sales low) 0.8572; 70% (Sales high) 0.2668; 100% (all new direct) -0.176
Sales' overlap is a proxy for direct loss, with no customer-level data behind it

claims.claim: 36% of 2028 direct profit lost, and exclusivity stops paying at 65% of volumes
CEO view: assumes no loss, yet the contract bars all new direct licensing
Ceiling: negative even at plan, which breaks even at 88% lost
How each bar is built: 2028 direct gross profit × share lost = direct profit lost, deducted per bar
evidence: $1,476K 2028 direct gross profit ($1.8M ARR × 82%)
30% share lost (Sales: 30–70%; ceiling 100%)
$443K direct profit lost
Bars start from 2028 contribution of $1.30M at plan and $0.53M at 65% (royalties less support and team)

claims.claim: Understated: the lost 2028 ARR recurs in 2029

slides.title: The growth case for exclusivity rests on correlation and an unbooked forecast, while what it gives up is certain

claims.claim: Competitor wins show correlation, not cause
evidence: 5 competitors cited by the CEO as proof
The five firms got more OEM marketing support than Boreal is offered
Their products were more mature when they signed
They already held more market share before exclusivity
Nothing isolates what exclusivity itself added

claims.claim: The volume is a forecast, not a booking
evidence: 14,000 robots called booked, with no purchase orders
The competitor deck calls the 2029 forecast "booked devices"
No customer has issued a purchase order
OEM quarterly shipment data are not independently audited
Royalties count only when robots ship, and cash arrives after a lag

claims.claim: The cost is Boreal's freedom to sell
evidence: $1.8M new direct ARR expected in 2028 in the territory
Bars direct licensing to new North American customers, even on other OEMs' robots
Conflicts with the integration firm's nonexclusive pilot offer
Runs three years and starts at signing, before certification
Existing direct contracts must stay outside it, or Boreal faces claims

slides.title: Why not at signing
The software is not production-ready yet: lab downtime ran at 2.4 times the OEM's limit, before any peak-load test

claims.claim: Below the OEM's production bar
evidence: 98.8% uptime in a 12-week lab trial on 60 robots
Run in a lab, not in a fully loaded warehouse
Collision-heavy peak conditions were not tested
Safe-stop performance is not yet documented

claims.claim: Plus documented safe stops at full load
evidence: 99.5% uptime the OEM requires for production acceptance
The board wants this proven in OEM hardware before irreversible exclusivity
The draft makes exclusivity effective at signing, before this test
The 2027 forecast assumes shipments before certification is done

claims.claim: Downtime has to fall by more than half
evidence: 2.4x trial downtime as a multiple of the downtime the OEM allows
Downtime = 100% − uptime: 1.2% in the trial against 0.5% allowed; small sample, so the multiple is indicative only
The $0.45M third-party assessment has not started
Engineering targets certification by September 2027
Any slip delays royalties under every option

slides.title: As drafted, the contract lacks six protections the board and counsel require before any exclusivity

claims.claim: Timing of exclusivity: draft is effective at signing, before certification; Boreal needs only after documented uptime and safety validation
evidence: Breaks a board condition / Exclusivity before certification is irreversible

claims.claim: Scope: draft is exclusive North American distribution; Boreal needs new OEM robot sales only; existing and other-OEM customers stay direct
evidence: Avoids contract claims

claims.claim: Shipment audit: no clear right to audit reported shipments; Boreal needs audit right over quarterly shipment reports
evidence: OEM data unaudited

claims.claim: Royalty floor: no minimum once the advance is used; Boreal needs minimum royalty floor for any exclusive period
evidence: Protects the price of exclusivity

claims.claim: Release: no release if the model is retired or certification slips; Boreal needs automatic release on either event
evidence: Caps the downside

claims.claim: Source code: no escrow; code reusable by the OEM; Boreal needs source code held in escrow, not handed over
evidence: Protects Boreal's IP

claims.claim: the OEM has not yet agreed to any of these terms
evidence: From legal counsel, the software team and the board's stated conditions in the briefing pack

slides.title: Boreal can fund a first year of OEM work without the advance, with $0.55M to spare above its liquidity buffer

claims.claim: The advance is not what makes the program affordable
evidence: $M: Unrestricted cash 4.9; Liquidity buffer 2.6; Safety assessment 0.45; Dedicated OEM team 0.9; Support, 5,000 robots 0.4; Left above buffer 0.55
Share of headroom used by year-one OEM costs 76.1% = ($0.45M + $0.90M + $0.40M) ÷ $2.3M
Conservative: a full year of team and support cost at 2027 plan volume, no royalty cash; the pack gives no operating burn beyond what the $2.6M buffer covers

claims.claim: Assessment: due under any OEM option
Advance risk: the OEM can demand an offset if royalties fall short
Thin cushion: new costs need board sign-off

normalized.extraction_notes: Slide 1 gives both "April 2027" in the subtitle and "2026-11-20" as a date line. Both are recorded as they appear. Slide 16's option table rates each option on four tests (Direct channel kept, Certified first, Volume verified, OEM royalty) with circle symbols on a Weak–Strong scale. The plain-text extraction left those cells empty, so the ratings could not be recovered. The 'base' series in the stacked charts on slides 5, 6 and 13 look like invisible offsets for waterfall charts, so they were not counted as evidence. The formula layouts on slides 8 and 15 (×, +, ÷, = symbols) were rebuilt from the order of the text blocks. The slide had no pictures to transcribe.
